title: Stewardship of creation (CCC 2415–2418)
hook: animals and the earth entrusted to our care

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seventh commandment: don't steal, pay what's fair, share what the earth gives. Your line was goods are for all. Did you tip or pay someone fairly? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-two.

A sister leaves for two weeks of work and hands over a leash and a watering can. Walk the dog, morning and night. The balcony plants, every other day. The dog isn't the sitter's. The plants aren't either. But for two weeks, whether they live and thrive is up to the one holding the leash. A good sitter checks the soil with a finger, notices if the dog stops eating, and never mistakes the spare key for permission to do whatever they like with the apartment. The Catechism places this inside the seventh commandment, the one about goods. Today's word is what it calls our place among the animals and the earth.
screen: `A LEASH AND A WATERING CAN.` → `THE DOG IS NOT YOURS.` → `TWO WEEKS IN YOUR CARE.`

segments.voice: Start in the garden. Genesis tells how God placed the man in paradise, in the Douay-Rheims wording, "to dress it, and to keep it." Two jobs: work it, and guard it. Set beside it, the earlier line about dominion, ruling over the fish and the birds, sounds different. Dominion, the Catechism says, is not absolute. It's a care handed to us, and it is limited by concern for our neighbors, including the people who come after us. It even asks for what it calls a religious respect for the integrity of creation. A steward, then, is the one holding the leash. Not the owner. The one entrusted. Next, the animals. The Catechism says animals are God's creatures, that he surrounds them with his providential care, and that by simply being, they bless him and give him glory. So people owe them kindness. It points to saints who treated animals gently, naming Francis of Assisi and Philip Neri. Proverbs puts it in one line: "The just regardeth the lives of his beasts." Then the hard edges, said plainly. The Catechism says animals may be used for food and clothing, and that medical experiments on them are acceptable within reasonable limits, if they help to care for or save human lives. And it says it is contrary to human dignity to cause animals to suffer or die needlessly. Finally, a balance. It's right to love animals, the Catechism says, but not to give them the love that is owed only to persons. And it notes that money spent on animals should not come first when people are in need. So stewardship holds two hands open: one for the creature in front of you, one for the neighbor you haven't met yet.
screen: `TO DRESS IT, AND TO KEEP IT.` · `DOMINION IS NOT ABSOLUTE.` · `ANIMALS GIVE GOD GLORY.` · `NO NEEDLESS SUFFERING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for an animal or a plant. If there's one near you, a dog asleep on the floor, a plant on the windowsill, go to it now. If not, bring one to mind. Settle, and breathe. Look at it as something entrusted, not owned. What does it need today? Water, a walk, a little shade, a clean bowl? Notice it without hurrying. If you pray, you can thank God for this one small creature. If you don't, just keep it company for the time. The bell holds the time.
Stewardship. Caring for what belongs to another: in Catholic teaching, the earth and its creatures, held in trust for God and for the neighbors who come after us. Today's word.
Your line: entrusted. Today, before you throw something out or walk past a thirsty plant, ask whose it really is, and who comes after you. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: The Catechism treats care for creation as part of the seventh commandment; some parishes bless animals on the feast of Saint Francis of Assisi, and some families teach children to care for pets and gardens as a duty to God.

fork.setup: you're looking after a sister's dog and plants for two weeks. the Catechism's word for your job is stewardship. which is closest?
options: they're yours to do with as you like.
you keep them well, for someone else.
you leave them alone and touch nothing.
fork.reveal: a steward is entrusted, not the owner. the Catechism says dominion over creation is not absolute; it's care, limited by concern for neighbors and those who come after.

original.note: Hebrew: to keep, to guard, to watch over — the verb behind "to keep it" in Genesis 2:15.

trapdoor: what you thought: dominion means the earth is ours to use up.
what it means: the earth and its creatures are entrusted to us, to work and to keep, with care for neighbors to come.
what a scholar hears: Genesis 2:15 gives two verbs, to work and to keep; the Catechism says dominion is limited by care for neighbors and for the generations to come.
